query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the grain size of the FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix will improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix
generation.mechanism: Increased surface hardness and mechanical strength due to finer grain size, leading to improved wear resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance compared to an unchanged coating in matched tests
generation.baseline: Unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix
generation.boundary: Grain size reduction within the range of fine-grained to ultra-nanocrystalline grain size
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between grain size and wear resistance in FeNiCrCoCu coatings is not fully understood and may depend on other factors such as composition and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear test with varied thermal and contact regimes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate of the FeNiCrCoCu coating with reduced grain size is not significantly lower than that of the unchanged coating, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. The fine-grained sample has higher surface hardness and mechanical strength, which is helpful to improve the wear resistance []. Compared with other materials, this can give us some inspiration for later work. The average wear rate of TiO2 10 wt.% NiAl coating deposited on the low alloy steel 40Cr4 surface is 9.821 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1, and the wear rate of TiO213 wt.% NiAl coating 40Cr4 is 1.22 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1 under the normal load of 10 N and sliding speed of 500 mm/s [], which is close to that of FG HEA under the load of 30 N and sliding speed of 5 mm/s. The wear rate of AlCrSiN-coated tool steel K340 is 5.681 × 10−7 mm3 N−1 m−1 under the load of 10 N and 10 cm/s []. The average wear rate of AlTiSiN + TiSiN coatings deposited on the H 13 tool steels is 2.30 × 10−8 and 1.31 × 10−8 mm3 N−1 m−1 for normal load of 30 and 50 N at the lubricated conditions, respectively []. Tubrication can effectively improve the wear resistance of materials, which presents good inspiration for our later work.

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.
